newsitem.title: UK: Eastern European bond calendar gets heavy.
newsitem.headline: Eastern European bond calendar gets heavy.

text.p: Borrowers in central and eastern Europe are lining up to tap international capital markets, but bankers say their need for funds may not be satisfied quickly.

The reason is not for lack of investor enthusiasm. On the contrary, they are more than ready to snap up issues that are higher-yielding than most bond markets. But the logistics of underwriting are slowing the process.

"The calendar is very heavy, but the problem with these (central and eastern) European borrowers is that they go dishing out mandates like school dinners," said a syndicate official at a U.S. bank in London.
"The borrowers, especially for a debut transaction, underestimate how much work has to be done," he added.
In the first half of this year, eastern European bond issuance jumped to $6.2 billion from $1.1 billion in same period a year ago, according to industry data.
Bankers see scope for another $6 billion by year-end, bringing the annual total to around $12 billion vs $3.7 billion for the whole of 1996.
Syndicate managers said many of these deals would take many months, rather than weeks, to arrange.
The deals are also delayed in order to acquire a credit rating, and some are held up by unforeseen political events.
Russia's debut bond, managed jointly by JP Morgan and SBC Warburg, took many months to surface.
Not that it prevents investment banks from fierce competition for a mandate. Many banks underwrite bonds with very small margins in order to establish themselves in the lucrative region.
CSFB, JP Morgan and SBC Warburg have each underwritten more than $1 billion in issues from the region this year.
On the sovereign front, Bucharest, Kazakhstan, Slovakia, Ukraine, Uzbekistan and Warsaw are all expected to launch deals this year.
In Russia alone, many regions, cities, companies and banks are waiting to raise money on the Euromarket, where their funding costs have been on steady decline.
The Komi Republic, the cities of Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, Oryl, Perm, Sakha, Samara, Sverdlovsk and the republic of Tatarstan are some of those keen to raise funds.
Bulgaria and Estonia also plan Eurobonds for 1998.
Borrowers favour this market for their ever-increasing funding needs as it enables them to extend debt maturity and access a broader yield-hungry investor base.
Bankers also said the region, in particular Russia, was seen as cheap compared with Latin American countries.

"The new-issue pipeline is growing exponentially at the moment. We understand there is a new mandate awarded every day. Investors are comfortable with the compensation they are getting for the risk," said a banker at ABN AMRO in Amsterdam.

Investors are also confident in the credit ratings and many believe certain borrowers deserve to be upgraded, particularly with a push toward European Union membership and general reform. There is market speculation that Russia might be upgraded later this year.
As the market is credit driven, it is not severely disrupted by volatility in emerging market currencies and recent jitters were soon shrugged off, dealers said.

The market took off after Russia's first Eurobond launched last November. The federation has since raised a total of $4.1 billion on international bond markets. Russia said it would borrow $3 billion to $3.5 billion from international bond markets in 1998.

The intense competition for capital and fear of crowding out by some of the more sought-after names could see borrowers seek funding elsewhere, such as in the syndicated loan or equity markets, bankers said. But the Euromarket was still most-desirable and first-time issuers could well take their time to launch.
Peter Schikaneder, director in global markets at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said future issuance would be driven by two factors -- interest rate stability and investors' quest for higher yields.
